summary: Experience report from a 14-week Java/Spring Boot project course (Osaka Institute of Technology, 2025: 14 students, 4 teams) that introduced spec-driven development with GitHub Copilot agent mode. The workflow has four phases: investigation, planning, implementation, review. A template repo carries copilot-instructions.md, specs.md, tasks.md and report folders. Data are weekly self-reported AI-usage surveys, added lines of code compared against the 2022-2024 cohorts, and instructors' weekly one-on-one ratings (0-3) of whether each student can explain their own committed code. Throughput rose versus earlier years, but it was confounded and mostly a 2024 effect. The association between AI usage and comprehension was not statistically significant.

claims.claim: AI usage patterns varied across development phases and teams
claims.evidence: Figure 4: weekly self-reported 0-4 usage by phase. All teams used AI for implementation and debugging. Investigation and planning use varied widely (Team 25D barely used it). Review-phase use was low for everyone. Descriptive, self-reported, 4 teams.

claims.claim: AI agent utilization increased implementation throughput
claims.evidence: Table 1 / Fig. 5: Steel-Dwass tests on added LOC per student per lecture across the 2022-2025 cohorts (38/28/25/14 students). Most significant pairs are 2022<2024 or 2023<2024. The SDD/agent year 2025 beats 2022 in only lec07 and lec10 and 2023 in lec08, and never differs significantly from 2024, when AI use was not recommended. There is no concurrent control, LOC is the metric, outliers above 1000 lines are not drawn, and AI-generated Markdown is excluded by hand. §5.2 concedes cohort confounding.

claims.claim: AI agent use tended to encourage students to proceed without fully understanding the code (abstract)
claims.evidence: Fig. 6 shows descriptive means: AI-level-3 students had low comprehension in lec09-10, and three teams dipped in lec09 when AI use peaked. The body states 'no clear statistical trend was confirmed' (§5.1) and 'this trend was not statistically significant' (§6). Ratings come from the same instructors who ran the intervention, unblinded, on a 0-3 scale.

claims.claim: Regular verification of code comprehension by instructors and feedback are essential for maintaining educational effectiveness
claims.evidence: There is no arm without interviews; every student was interviewed weekly. The argument is a lec09 dip followed by lec10 recovery that coincides with feedback, and a non-significant null attributed to the intervention.

claims.claim: Standardised templates (copilot-instructions.md, spec templates, rules) helped students start smoothly
claims.evidence: Instructors' impression ('appeared to help'); no measurement.

patterns.note: The 'investigation' phase replaces requirements analysis: before planning, the agent writes a report on how the current code would support the feature (docs/reports/investigate). Uptake varied greatly by team (Fig. 4). No outcome comparison between teams that did and did not investigate.

Weekly one-on-one 'explain your committed code' checks rated 0-3 by instructors. The association between AI usage and comprehension was not significant (n=14, large SEM). The recovery after the lec09 dip is read as an intervention effect, but there is no group without the checks, so this is not an isolating comparison.
Kiro-style SDD adapted to investigation, planning (tasks.md), implementation (specs.md updated) and review, run with Copilot agent mode. Not compared against a non-SDD workflow in the same year.
copilot-instructions.md in the template holds the workflow and project rules (Japanese output, conventions). Not evaluated.
Students must review and be able to explain each AI artifact. The review phase saw the lowest AI usage.
An AI review phase generates review reports (functionality, security, quality, docs consistency). It was rarely used and not evaluated.

methodology.sample: 14 students in 4 teams (2025) for RQ1/RQ3; 2022-2025 cohorts (38/28/25/14 students) for the LOC comparison
methodology.baselines: Historical cohorts only (2022: assumed no AI; 2023-2024: AI not recommended); no concurrent control
methodology.models: GitHub Copilot agent mode; underlying model not stated; students could also use any other AI service
methodology.variance: Box plots, Steel-Dwass multiple comparisons per lecture, SEM mentioned as large; no effect sizes or correlation coefficients for RQ3

standards.artifacts: Instructors' demo project on GitHub (Japanese) and example prompts in Fig. 3; student data, survey instrument details and analysis scripts not released

biases.detail: 14 students and 4 teams; the authors acknowledge low statistical power.
AI usage is a weekly self-reported 0-4 perceived-helpfulness score, which mixes use and perceived value.
Comprehension was rated by the instructors who designed and delivered the intervention, unblinded to AI usage.
Added LOC stands in for throughput; authors acknowledge it misses design, refactoring and deletions.
Elective course; the 2025 cohort is less than half the 2022 cohort; year-to-year cohort differences confound the LOC trend.
The abstract says the study 'demonstrates' that instructor verification is 'essential', which no comparison supports.

verdict_reason: Peer-reviewed, honest threats-to-validity section, and on-topic (Java/Spring Boot, SDD with an explicit pre-plan investigation phase, comprehension checks). The quantitative evidence is weak: n=14, historical controls, LOC, self-report, unblinded ratings. The abstract's comprehension and 'essential' claims go beyond the body's own non-significant result. Admit as an experience report, not as evidence that the safeguards work.
applicability: Closest match in this batch to the team's rollout: Java/Spring Boot, spec-driven, Copilot-style instructions, and an agent-written investigation report required before planning. Usable as design input, not evidence. (1) Make the pre-spec investigation report a first-class artifact. Uptake varied a lot by team, so the harness should check the report exists before planning rather than trust the process doc. (2) Add a lightweight comprehension check: the developer explains the AI-written change in a PR or a short walkthrough. This paper cannot show the check works, only that dips were visible because someone looked. (3) Students are not professionals, and LOC is not a productivity measure; do not quote the throughput result.

conflicts_with.detail: A controlled between-subjects study (54 students) finds agent users score much lower on comprehension of their own code. Here the AI-usage/comprehension association is not significant (n=14, with weekly instructor interviews). This could be low power or an intervention effect; neither paper isolates the interview safeguard.
